HARRY Gaawam As A Wisann.—Before I joined the circuit of the younger Ginnett, of circus celebrity, err 1860, I had made the acquaintance of several members of the !company travelling with Mr. (Armen's father. Poorly in the spring of 1859 some looniness took too into the neigh- bourhood of Whitechapel, end while passing the London Apprentim public-house, I heard my name shouted, and, j looking round, espied Harry Graham, whom I had known as a clown in the elder Ginnetes circus. He wan doing a conjuriog trick outside a miserable booth, at the mine time inviting the public to walk in, the charge toeing one half- penny. On the completion of the trick he jumped otf the platform, and insisted upon adjourning to the puhlic-houne, where he explained the didiculty he was in through having been laid up all the winter with rheumatic gout. On his partial recovery, he was compelled to accept the first thing that offered, which was an engagement with the owner of the booth, it man known in the profession as the "Dudley demon." Poor Harry begged me to give him a start: an, knowing hint to loealaorhoondatooonjooringtoicks,lo,omnto an arrangement to take him through the provinces as M. Phillipi the Wizard. Thin was on a Friday. On the fol- lowing Wednesday, no quickly had our arrangements been !completed, my conjuror appeared at Rantsgate to morning and evening twrforiiimem ; the former netting eighteen pounds and the latter fourteen pounds ; our prices being ' three shillings,. two shillings, and one ahilling. Yet, in Whitechapel this same noon would not have earned five chitlings a clay ! Among other places we visited was Dart- ford, where I took tbe Bull Hotel assembly-mom, which had been recently built, but not yet opened. Mrs. S—, a lady of considerahle distinction, kindly gave me her patronage, and I arranged for a band from Gravesend. On the day of the performance, towards Cie afternoon, as the band had not arrived, I sent guy assistant to Graymend with instructions to bring the nmici.ilis with him. At half-past seven, the time announced for opening the doors, a large crowd had assembled, an out of curiosity to see the new room as to witness the performances to in a short time every seat was occupied. Just before the clock struck eight—the time for commencement—my assistant came runhing in with the intelligence that the hand had gone to Dover too perma- nent engagement. I ran round to the stage-door and told Graham. He mid it was impossible to give the entertain- ment without nuliie of soote sort to carry it off. In my despair I rushed into the street, intending to go to Reeve, the music-seller and hire a pianoforte. But I had not gone far when I limrol a 'tweaking noise, which, upon approach- ing closer, I found to proceed from three very dirty little German h0y,,,,a1e pLiving a cornopean, another a trombone, and the third a Itigeolet. On accoating them, I found they could not speak a word of English, so I took two of them by the arms and dragged thou along, leaving the other to follow hie companions to their fate. On reaching the build- ing I could hear the impatient audience making a noise for a start. Harry Crraham, on seeing my musicians, said it would upset everything to tHom hem to be M sight of the audience. 01 can manage that," I mid; 'coo will just put them under the stage, and I will rnotion them when to strike up and when to lmve off." In another moment M. Phillipi moron the stage, and received with shouts by the audience. At the conclusion of the performance I went to the front and thanked my patronees, Mrs. B—, for her kindness. "Ah !" said that lady, "he Is very clever. But oh ! that horrid unmrthly music Montague's Recollections of an Equestrian Manager."

—.F.TTonNecon era kftwormi.—There has never been in this country a more destructive tornado than that which recently swept ~ver the State of Missouri. While the cable , has given you the full story of its appalling loss of life, ' there are some incidenta of deep interest that have since been made known and attracted much attention. The tor, mdo moved in a north-easterly direction along tile valley of the Jameo river, and almost annihilated the town of Marshfield. An infant aged 10 months, whose mother had , twen killed and all It. friends injured, their house being blown to atoms, was carried by the wind to the north of the town, and was found next naorning in a ravine there.l llt is doing well. Another child, aged two years, was found • next morning in the forks of a tree, where it had been nearly 24 hours. It was considerably bruised, but will recover. This child had been carried from its home three niilto dim hint, its parents having given it up for lost A waggon woo carried four nsil. by the wind and was found in com- parausely good condition. A section of the smoke-stack ~f a mill wan carried three mile, and a half. A meteorological 'investigation of the tornado shows that everywhere along its track there is evidence of a wave of water flowing in the I rear of, the cloud-spouts, and in a direction towards the centre and upwards. At some ;daces the debri, showing tbia wave are carried ap nod over obstructions . high as three feet. These currents flowed in greater volume up hills, in mane localities w.hing out the entire top-soil. Fibrous roots and grass tuft, show their direction to have I been up-hill, and they came frim all points of the compass I towards the top of the hill where the tornado was at the tune raging. No traces can tre found of th.e currents flow- ing down-hill. Their force is /Mown by many level places being swept clean of mil. Leaves, grass, timber, and the dahris of deetroyed buildings, carried along by the current, and left in its track, all arranged themselvne longitudinally to the current. In testimony of this ware the statement of George Oiltiert a residence of Marshfield, is given. Ile land his family were visiting about eight nules in the court. try,.d the centre of the tornado passed within a few yards of where they were. A wave of water, apparently 16 feet high rolled in the tmr of the te,int of contact of ihe cloud. spout with the earth. It rolled over them in a second, drenched them completely, and was cold as ice. There have been 150 deaths from this tornado in ?danshfield and the ad- jacent country, while other storms at the same time killed many to ore over a wile expanse of territory stretching front Missouri to the Lakes.—Trines. Mug von Fowts.—Since milk is the only article of tout I known to contain within itself all the elementa necesaary to ! the perfection of growth and vigour in au animal, it is not strange that it thould be found to be one of the very best egg producing materials that can lot supplied to poultry. Given two flocks of fowls, and treatment, location, and original stock beingfequal In all respects save one, it will be found tlmt Mow having skimmed milk as a portion of their daily food or driuk:will give ntore eggs weekly, and for a longer term of weeks, th n those whose treatment is exactly the sante, with this stogie exception. A correspondent writes thus —"A! neighbour of ours, whose hens, to our exaspera. lion, kept laying on when eggs were 45 cents per doe., while ount persistently laid off during the same season, on being questioned revealed the fact that his hens had a pailful of skimmed, perhaps clabbered, milk uch day, and no other drink. On coimmring notes we each found that our manage- ment of .r fowls lent almost exactly alike, with this single difference—a difference that put many a dollar to the credit side of his ledger, while our own was left blank during the P3lHe period—and this thing had bema going on for y.rs, with the result always in favour of a milk diet." In cases where milk is very plentiful, and only it portion is neatest for fowls, it would be well, wiy once week or oftener, to give the milk in fornmnofeurdbyinootiogitonniithewhey separates front the more solid !salons. WHY MILK Sonts—ek writer inn the Throat° Globe asks this,—" Does the honsekeeper ever stop to ask herself or anyone else the question, what causes milk to rotor P It is by observing, taking note of the phenomena and occurrences of life' and studying or inquiring into their causes that It we gain nowledge. Must people have a kind of vague notion that milk sours from an inherent tendency ill its nature or composition, or in other words, from natu.ral depravity. But this inn misMke. Were there not external causes of change and decay, there is no reason why milk should not keep sweet for an indefinite period. °them suppose its souring and decay is emsntf Inc the :itmorphere, but there is nothing in the pure, unadulterated atowsphere to cause anything to decompose :Ind decay. The atmosphere perval. all no- tore, and is the greit sustainer of life. Milk is a perfect food, containing all the material/I for the development of all the various organs ond compounds of a young animal. Let useve what it it composed of trig pan of fresh cow's milk conttins—water, 88111; casein, 4,2; run, sugar, 335; butter, 3-00; salts, 0.45. By standing, the globules of but. ter, enveloped in to thin membrane of casein, rite to the stir- , face, forming the cream, but there is no r..n why the vramr, sugar, casein, and .IU should not remain pure for ever in contact with pure air only. Whence comes, then, the insidious foe that brings decay and putrefaction to this life-sustainieg compound? It contno front the air, but it is not of it. It is a vegetable substance, a fungus whose minute, , invisible seeds or spores are floating in the atmosphere. Some of these enter the milk, probably, as soon as drawn front the cow, and the warmth of the milk mut the presence of nitrogen in the casein furnish the necessary conditions for the growth of these germs or ferments, HMI fermentation ensues. The fermentation causes the disarrangement of the constituents of the sugar, changing it into alcohol and ladie arid, and this is sour milk. T/mt is the absorption of spores from the atmosphere which causes the milk to sour may be proved by heating the milk to boiling point, than killing the germs, and then canning it, excluding the air, when it will keep for an indefinite period. That jolt the fungus 'Tor. floating in the air, and not the air itself, that cawet the souring of the milk, has been liroved by connecting a long tube filled with cotton with the canned milk. The air will rind its way through the cotton and Piller the milk, but the spores will be arrested, and the milk remain sweet." DERBYSHIRE CIIEESE MAKING SYSTEM. The essential character of Derby cheese is that of a middle-class cheme ; it in not in any sense a fancy cheese 39 the Stilton and the Miracle and many of the Continental lobe.. are, hut it is 3 good substantial food; it does not app.l to the suffrages of the. upper ten," and its consump- lion has been mainly confined to the middle .d the lower climes of the people and to special districts within the limits of the British islands. Yet a first-clam Derby will not unfavourably compare with 0 firstmlass cheese of most 1 other English takes. The method on which Derby cheese , is nude is less complicati‘l that that ,if most other kinds; the appliances in use are fewer and simpler, and the dairy premises are umally of a more primitive character. It in not common tiva eh. cfl,na.o ...de on.ne than onoo a day, though we have known cares where careful dairymaids have made it twice a day during the whole of the summer ; these have considered, and with troth, that ch.mr is all the bet, if mule from tnilk that is quite fresh and sweet, which it not always is when it is twelve or fourteen hours old in warm weather ; and onn this method the cheese hu ! the further advantage of retaining all the cream of the milk. This, however, hot been found to be, or has been sapposed , to he, A disadvanmge onn Lind 111. has been highly farmed ; full-milk cheese has been found very liable to crack and heave, and be generally unmanageable, and dairymaids hme been driven for relief to the sure expedient of skimming a ; portion of the milk. tome well known that milk produced on highlrfarmed land, and by th,• consumption of “ke and corn, is richer in fats than milk that is produced from sound old puture land that has not been improved by high.farming ; and it is more than suspected that this increase In fats imports into the cheese some occult element or other that is very unmanage. able at times ; the additional butter obtained by these arti- finial aids does not appear to be balanced by a corrmpond• ingly increased percentage of the nitrogenous constituents of milk; and as the Derbyshire system of cheese-making is essentially a w eweet-curd " system this distorteince of the 1 normal balance uf milk-constituents Inas the effect in many caam of hastening the decay of the cheese. It inay be ob. jected here that the Stilton system of cheese-making ie' essentially one that disturbs the normal balance of the milk- constituents, by putting ,th extra quantity of cream into the milk from which the cheese is made, to this we would reply that Stilton cheese can only be made with entire success fnnnn sound old pasture land, without artificial aids, and that the Stilton system admits of the development of acidity in the cunl, which it. gr.t help in causing cheese to be more manageable. In no dairying district in the Islands has, we believe, the land beot more iinproved than in Derbyshire, and in that county it is commonly hollered to boot all events expedient to skim a portion of the milk, in order that the cheese may w stand" better, and that it may not bulge and crack, or beconne otherwise unmet/age- able.

--The old-fashioned circular floor beam" cheese-kellle" is generally used in Derbyshire farmhouses, and the cheese is usually made in the ordinary kitchen of the house ; it it seldom that a room is provided specially for making the cheese in, and the equipment generally is less finished than in certain other districts ; nevertheless, great improvements in these matters have bren brought about in the past twenty or thirty years. Though we have seen in use within a re- cent period various datry utensils of wood, and even a cheese-tub of the sante =aerial—hence the name—wood is now ahnost wholly discarded, and tin, or brass, or glued earthenware, as the case may be, his taken its place. The vessel in which the milk is coagulated is generally of tin, though sometimes of brans, the milking-pails are no longer of wood, but of tin, ardent in very conservative establish- ments, and the pant in which the Milk is set to Ormin are of glued earthenware or of tin. When the manufacture of malleable glass is a success, that will be the best material of which the 1.-mentioned vesaels can be made. . . . Not uncommonly it is left out of doors, if it is likely to be cooler there, and is covered upon keep intruders out of it. In other cases loin sieved into shallow tin or mrthen- ware pans, where, being in smaller bulk, it is likelier to re- main sweet through the night. In either cane a portion of the cream that has risen during the night, and somethum the whole of it, is skimmed off on the following morning, after which the morning's milk is mired with the evening's, and the whole mass is rained or lowered, as the case my be, to SOdeg. ITALY. The latest report from Rome Otto the result of the Italian ' election strengthens the belief that the Government will have a majortiy in the new Parliament. Rowe., Thursday. The Opinions, in • leading article to.day, explains the reasons for the sympathy felt for Mr. Gladstone by the Italian people, and points out that when the right honourable gentleman was in Opposition he de- manded that satisfaction should he given to the claims of Greece, urging that such a policy, combined with the complete autonomy of Servia. Roumania, and Montenegro, would diminish the excessive preponderance of Austria. Germany, and 1111K(Sic. Then- is reason to believe that, should Italy now propose to take formal possession of the Ray of Assad, no opposition would be raised by Sir Augustus Paget as during Loni Beaconsfield's Administration.

AFG'HANISTAN. A telegram was received on Thursday as the India Office from the Viceroy stating that General Stewart reported all quiet in Logan and Kohietan. General Robert's force had destroyed the forts of Padshah Khan, a Ghazal chief. 2,000 Sagis, who were making hostile demonstrations, had been attacked by a British force from Jellalabad, and defeated with great loss. An naofficial telegram from Cabot states that Abbe Rahman Khan has dismissed his army, stating that at present there is no occasion for any hostile operations against the British.

Such as are canonical are deetned eufficient by the ecclesiastical laws to avoid the marriage in the spiritual court ; but these in nor law only make the mart iage voidade, and not ipso facto coil, until sentence of nullity be obtained. 1/f this nature are pre-contract, con- sanguinity, or relation by blood and :titinity, or relation by marriage ; and soono particular corporal infirmities. And these canonical disabilities are either grounded upon the express wonls of the 3ivine law, or are consequences plainly deducible from them it therefore being aloha in the per- sons, who labour nyder them, to attempt to contract matri- mony together, they are properly the objects of the ecclesi- astical magistrates' tender; in order to separate the ofienders, and inflict penance for the offence, pro salute anitmartun. But such marriages not being void oh ioitio, but voidable only by the sergence of separation, they are eateetned valid to all civil purposes, unless such separation is actually made during the Ete of the parties. For, after Olin death of either of them, the courts of common law will not suffer the spiritual court to tleclare such marriages to hove !teen void ; because suet declaration cannot now tend to it reformation of the parties These canonical disabili- ties being entirely the province of the ecclesiastical courts, our books are perfectly silent concerning them. Hut there are a few statutes. which serve as tiirectories to threw courts. at which it will be proper to take notice It, statute 32 Her.. VIII., c. it, it is &claret, that all persons may lawfully marry, but each as are prohibited by God's law and thtit all marriages contracted by 11.11 fill persons in the face of the ellen h, and consummated with bodily knowledge, and fruit of children, shall be indissoluble. And !because in the time of popery a great variety of degrees of kindred were made impedimenta to marriage, which impediments might however be bought MY for money) it is &claretl by the same statute, that nothing ,Ciott's law excepted! shall impeach any mar- riage but within the Levitical degrees; the farthest of which is that between uncle and niece. Ott" the prohibit,l dry,,,—Marringe is pro- hibited under the fourth degree of consanguinity according to the civil law, except in the ascending or descending line. It is scarcely possible, however, that any one !Mould marry Ins issue in the fourth degrte. Between collateral brarches, all who are in the fourth, or any higher degree, are permitted I to marry. Thus rust cousins are in the fourth ringers; a nephew and great aunt are in the f.mrth degree, and, though ! a man tnay Oct marry his grandmother, he may marry her sister. These rules apply to the same degrees of affinity by marriage ; but the affinity must he in a direct line: thus the relations by consanguinity of the husband are not related to thew, of the wife, atid consequently two brothers may marry twt sisters; or • father and son a mother and daughter."

It ie sail and no doubt with a good deal of truth, that the trade of a cooper must have Men coeval with the dawn of history, it being of the first necearity for, humble as the trade seeme, the art of coopering has enabled men to possess and retain the richest viands of modern climes; it promotes and facilitates the export and import of the produce of dis- tant countries. It has enriched the merchant, supplied the wants and luxuriee of the people, augmented the public revenue of all civilised countriek end giving spirit to navigation. There are different sorts of coopers. There is the butt-cooper. who manufactures all kinds of wire for breweries, &c., also puncheons and hogs- heads for distilleries. The dry-cooper manufactures hogs- teadaand casks for containing every kiml of dry produce, the ; leading feature of the employment in hie line being the making of hogsheads for sugar. The white-cooper produces all ouch domestic utensils ikr are used in private brewing, washing, and deiriee—such as churns, Pads, and everY con- venience required for the multiplicsl purposes of domestic economy. , I should recontmend "M. R., Winsford," to read the . article on Chivalry in the Encyclopedia Britannica. where , he will find much to interest him. Perhaps for his pur. . pow it may be sufficient to say that in what are known as ; chive] mum,' but Li:ideal-me times, there existed what was , , known as the" wager of battle." Penton. of all degrees had • the right to appeal to arms to terminate certain suite, wrongs, and misunderstandings. A near relative of a person who hod been slain could challenge to combat with wespons a supposed murderer, although a jury might have acquitted him. Both Sir Walter Scott, in his Ivanhoe, and Shakspere, allude to the custom. 'The Royal Championship of Eng- land rests on the foundation of this ancient appeal. The "manger of battle" custotn eras abolished by the Act 59 George Itt, cap. 411, but the Royal Championship was re- tained and still exists, and is likely to do no long as there le "a consideration "at the back of it. The whole thing is a piece of tomfoolery as looked at through modern spectacles. In the dark ages. when a King's person was supposed to be more precious than that of say of his subjects, Kingly veto...showed itself by deputy. On the corona,iou day a Knight, Armed to the teeth, m.le forth and off,reil to fi,ht anyone thee the newly-created King was the true and I.twful heir to the King. The manor of Scrivelsby was given for the service rendered by this royal champion. The manor is now held by a family that has held it for centuries, and in the event •f the Prince of Wales coining t.i the throne the possessor of the manor will, in keeping with this idiotic custom, arm himself to the teeth and challenge anyone to fight who glenies that the l'rince is not the lawful heir to the Kingdom. J. M. Angtsrgau, St. Helens. Since the coronation of Richargl 11. (1377) the office of Royal Champion has been held by • Dymoke, the heal of the family of that name, who has held tlie manor of Scrivelsb,,, in Lincolnshire, worth about 21,200 per annum, by the tenure of this service. During the reigns of Edwards It. and 111. the right was in dispute, and from the days of the Conqueror it was vested in the far-farned fsmily of Mar- mice, whose chief clone from Normandy with Duke William, and is supposed to have held Scrivelsby on condition of per- forming the service of Champion "Coronation Anecdotes; or select and interesting fragments of English Coronation Ceremonies," by Giles Gossip, Esq., gives • circumstantial account of the proceedings of the Royal Champion on the occasion of the coronation of George the Fourth. After the King had been crowned in Westminster Abbey and hod re- turned to Westminster Hall, the Royal Champion made his appearance in the Hall at the sound of trumpet. at least his deputy did. He Was accompanied by the Deputy Earl Mambal, the Lord High Constable, and a host of attendants, and was attired in A complete suit of bright armour. He read from a paper a challenge to fight anyone who denied that the King was the rightful heir to the throne. Of course nobaly ampted the challenge. E. JOHNSON, Runcorn. 58.—Haroterrs.

ASSAULT.° • POLICE OFFICER AT A SITTON°N-MAAER- riat.o.—Thomas Mann, a Staffordshire ironworker, employed at Ince, was charged before Mr. Houghton, at Lorton, on Tuesday, with assaulting Constable Walrnsley. at Park-lane, Aehton-in-Makerfield, on Sunday. On Sunday afternoon the prisoner and about ten other ironworker, attacked the constable without any provocation, knocked him down, and afterwards kicked him. The prisoner was remanded to Wigan County Police-court. lisennarion GROUND FOR Aswrow.—On Monday the township of Ashton was en fete on the occasion of the formal opening of the recreation ground which has been placed at the disposal of the inhabitants by Lord Gerard. This ie the Little Town Field," situate in the centre of the township, and in every way adapted for the purposes of a recreation ground. The field is nearly eightaeres in extent, and, beaides being conveniently accessible, has an even sur- face, and commands a good view of the sortounding neigh- bourlimal. A committee appointed at a public meeting. I having Mr. Valiant ss their chairman and Mr. Fairless as their honorary monetary, proceeded to collect eubscriptions to defray the expenseof laying out the ground, and up to the preeent time there has been received in monetary con- tributions £155 On. 6d. Tradesmen hare also contributed something like £2O worth of materials., and workingmen, unable to give money or Lind, have willingly given their lab-oar, which is estimated at about £24, making the total contributions in round numbers £3OO. There has been ex- ponied £194, and it is mtimated that about .Cl5O more will be required, that making the outlay on the ground nearly .C 3.10. A capital bowling green has been laid, and there are also portions of the ground set apart for cricket, quoits, and footfall. Eighty gentlemen have given in their names as member,, and it is hoped that now the field is ready for nee this number will be largely augmented. The formal open- ing on Monday was celebrated by the holding Otto athletic festival, which was • great Carcase, upwards of 3100 people being present to witnem the sports. At the 'Town Hall a procession was formed, which headed by the band of the Lancashire Hammond the clergy and ministers of all dea nominations, together with the members of the Local Board, the committee, and the inhabimnts and friend.. Arrived at the ground most of the gentlemen named ascended the grandstand. Mr. Monhert, agent to ford Gerard, declared the ground open. and a vote of thanks wee accorded to Lord (horned. The company then adjourned to witness the athletic sports. The day being fine the proceedings were very successful, no less than £5O being taken at the gate. Scott hue made a valuable contribution to the discuseion of our agri- cultural prompects, a subject which is causing considerable anxiety on account of the low temperature and the drought. Mr. Scott does cot think that any confirmed injury has yet heen done to the growing crops except on thorny lightest lands, and be points out that springs even later than the pre- sent have generally la.nn followed by prosperous agricultural years. Against the thinness and lateness of the wheat plant he sets the fact that premature luxuriance never precedes a good crop. The main drawback to this year's probable agricultural prosperity is the foulness of the land, and Mr. Scott hold, that there are now only two ways of dealing with land in this country either by permanently improving it, to be followed by high farming under secure conditions, or allowing it to go out of cultivation. Tux FOREIGN COM TEMIM.—The new tariffs for coal ! carried over the railways between the Dortmund mining district and the North Sea ports has now been published. For consignments to Hamburg the former rate of £3. 10s. for 10,M0 kilos (say 10 tone) is reduced to £3. The reduction applien not only to consignments of coal destined for export, but also to cool for home consumption. A reduction to the extent of 4s. for the sarnequantity on the line from Hamburg to Lubeck hue aleo been promised by the directors of the Laibeck-Buchen Railway Cmnpany, no that the total reduction from the N'estphalian pits to the Baltic ports will be 14, per 10 tons. A reduction of toe. per 10 tone has been made likewise for coal destined for Bremen ; but in this case the conceeeion applies only t. cool for export or for consumption on ocean-going steamers. The new tariffs are provisionally to remain in force for One year.

The original demand of the operatives was for an advance of 50c. per day. At Roubaix theempinyers refuse to negotiate with the operatives until a sufficient number have returned to week to sat tie I.ms in motion at all the mills. Addi- tional strikes in the linen industry of the Lille and Artnen- tit,ce district are reported. About 2,000 operatives have turned not at Vastmehal and Hall uin,and 1,500 at Houpliges. The crops of 1079, compared with those in 1078, show a total decrease in cereals of 09,654 acres; oats having decreased by 82,584 acres, or 5.8 per cent. In the preceeding year thedacrease was 63,327 acres,or 4.3 per cent— and here and rye by 1,799 Acres, while wheat increased ' 3.470 acres, Neley by 10,6108 acres, and beans and peas by 571 ore... In green crops there is a total decrease of 23,173 acres, potatoes having decreased by 4,041 acres, against a decrease 07 20.570 acres in the previous year ; turnins by 15,546 acree, cabbage by 6,0110 acres, vetches and rape by 2,541 acres, and carrots. parsnips, and other green crops by 921 acres, while mangel wurzel and beet root increased by 5,936 acres. Flax shows an increase of 16,204 acres, and meadow and clover a decrease of 5,549 acres. In 1879, 345 acres in every 1I under crops were under cereals, 25.2 under green crepe, 2 5 under flax, and 37.8 under meadow and clover. In crops a decrease has taken place in ten years of front 5.641,140 acres in 1870 to 5,121,833 acres in 1879, or from 278 to 25.2 per cent of the total area. Ton Queen's Speech, or which would be more appropriately deeignated the Government's Pro. sesame, was reed by the Lord Chancellor in the Home of Lords on Thereday, and on that day the new Parliament practieally commenced the business of tie. mission. Before the delivery of the speech the mew feesshadewed pee., ateuretely what had to come, and the public were put into poweesion of the chief feat area of the speech ere it underwent its formel delivery through the medium of the occupant of the Woolsack. After an allusion to the temporary ad. journment rendered needful by the Minieteria . appointments, the Queen declares that her relation with all foreign Powers are friendly ; and turning to the East. she alludes to the necessity of enforcing her policy of ineisting, in concert with other Power., on the fulfilment of the uncompleted portion of the Berlin Treaty. The promotion of that Eonopa,n concert, which the late Government so unfortumtely broke up in the earlier stegee of the Eastern Question, in, to be a prime concern of the new Government; and the intootiou to rusty out, at last, the territorial arrange. meets to which that Treaty gave European sanction will he exceedingly gratifying to the Greeks. The tide of emigration still flows on unchecked, and thinking people are beginning to rampart that something is amiss when people are compelled to leave their fatherland in Intake in quest of opportunities for earning a subsistence in other climes. Mr. James Caird, the eminent agrieulturiat, draws attention to the fact that in this large °frothns is a great number of agrieultitrists, and he very timely draws the attention of those tillers of the soil who have not yet left the coasts of their native land in despair to the course they ought to follow to maintain their position in the feee of the altered circutnetancea in which they have been placed by the large and constant influx of foreign produce. Mr. Csird deala with the ambient in no half-hearted fashion, and makes BO attempt to hide painful truths. He lays the axe at the root of our premier land laws ; points out that landowners, as well as tenants and labourers, will have to realise the fact that freedom of cultivation, with coinpensation for unexhaaated improvements in holdings, will have to be grantid ; and urges that a complete revolu• Mon in farming will have to take place. The reporte of the deputation of farmers who recently visited various parts of the Canadian Dominion, and the competition that not only Canada, but America and other places, offers to the British agricalturists in Eng!lab markets enforce the fact that farmem in this country mast give way to their colonial and American rivals in the growing of many of the crops that British agriculturists have hitherto chiefly depended upon, and betake themssivee to the growing of such produce se cannot be reoeived from distant lands before it perishes. He draws the attention of his fellow-agriculturists to the fact that the United States predates twice as much corn as France and the United Kingdom put together, that corn-growing territory in the States is practically unlimited, and that North-Western Canada pmeesees a tract of country stretching seven hundred miles heresn the mntinent which can be brought ander tillage, and be made to influence the markets of the world by the extent of the itflux of its produce. A great teeter in the consideration of the .mpetition which Canada is likely to give is the cheapneaa of the land in the Dominion, and the fertility of the soil ; whilst the genial influence of the American climate, au! prootiol inexhamtibihty of ite virgin lands, aro not tt be lost sight of. Auotlier feature is that these lands, 60 well adapted for wheat growing, are capable of producing as much grain per acre without the resistance of manure an our partially-exhaunted lands can be made to grow with the aid of all the artificial manures that °herniate can devise or invent. With them facts staring them in the face, Mr. Caird urge. that English farmers will have to abandon that mode of farming which their fathers and grandfathers put.. sued, and mark out for themeelvee a line of proce- dure more in conmnmee with the necessities of the time, There are many articles of produce that neither Amelicana nor Canadians could hope to transmit to this country before they perished. These are articles the English public demand, and are such that no foreign effort san supply. English farmer., we imagine, will not be slow to recognise that, with freedom of cultivation, their attention in the future must be devoted to supplying the home markets ' with such produce as agriculturalists beyond the seas cannot furnish.

There chances, however, to be a "oar" 10 11,5 Runcorn Market, and it happened that recently two spirited young fellows, who no doubt considered themselves smart It fisticuffs, and having one or more grievancesto settle, did "wit to the ear," and did pummel tech other. Club came :Irom a source usually Rand reliable, but it turns out that the w hole of the members of the club deny all knowledge of the "set to," and, .1 can quite an- , &regrind that they must feel some annoyance even at a ! facetious paragraph accusinw two of their body of having noire to the ear," and as your humble eervarn has no wish to wooed the suscepti- bilities of the most resned, he must fall on his marrowbones and cry in this instance " Peccevi." I The special meeting of the Runcorn Commissioners, held for the purpose of coneidering what action eLould he taken in relation to the Liverpool Corporation Water Bill, proved a singular and somewhat stormy gathering. I understand that it is alleged by those gentlemen who were parties to the equisition calling the special meeting, that it is of the highest importance that Runcorn should Lake proceedings for obtaining a legal standing in case the commiesionere , desire to oppose the passing of the Bill, except on condition ' that certain concessions were granted to the town. All the efforts of members to get the question in dispute fairly die- C 1191.11 proved futile, as certain gentlemen threw obstaclee in the path, and objected to the couree which had been pursued by the requisitionists. Dr. Nlthougall fell foul of the law clerk (Mr. W. It. Linaker,) through urging the chairman (Mr. W. Lyon.) to exercise his own judgement mato whether the Bill could or could not be considered at the meeting, land not be dictated to by the Clerk. This scents to have I caused quite a scene, Mr. Linaker strongly denying any intention on his part to dictate to the chair, and declining to be spoken to in such a manner. At thin juncture 1/r. McDougall reminded Mr. Linaker that be was a member of the Board, which was rrmt by the rejoinder that it would he well if he would keep Ins place m such. It required all the roe bootie' of the chairmen to throw 0:1 on the troubled water., and permit the busluess to proceed. Mn. Norman seems to have been in quite Fgyptian doh,. near to whet wee going on, and described hie condition as that of one who // was ewimming about somewhere." A new member of the Board—Mr. Frith—made the confueion worse confounded by asking very am kwanl question. to the effect whether anything could be done in the matter under dispute until a previous resolution had been rescinded. Mr. Iland/ey tventured to um the famous phrase of the late Pope and College of Cardinale, boo posso 'tato, upon which Dr. McDougall dropped upon him like a hawk, and wverely twitted hitn for airing hie Latin amongst , such a body of gentlemen. I, how.ver, was some- what astonished to see from the report that in the course of his reply, the :doctor himself quoted the Latin word. tortes stood, which was somewhat awkward, to can the least of it, under the circumerancvs. At all meet- ings of Town Councils at which Boards of Commiesionere tree merely humble imitation, the legal authoeito to whom appeal is always made is the Town Clerk, (or what is known M Runcorn ae the Law Clerk,) and in him I. vested , the power of ruling as to the proper muse of proceeding in any such matmrs as the one which wart being dealt with at the time when Dr. McDougal made Inc remark about dictation. To tell the Chairman not to be dictated to by the legal adviser of the Board, is certainly an original if not a very prudent kind of address. I wonder what the Doctor himself would hove said if he hAI been acting es Law Clerk at the time. To my mind the ehort epeech made by Mr. Mendowcroft, in which he criticised the action of Mr. Philip Spmkomn in causing the members i to be called together, entl then declining to unburden his mind of what he tad to communicate, when genLemen, many of them engaged in business, had come there at great inconvenience, wae marked by touch common Renee. Mr. Speakman, however, is blessed vrlth considerable tact end ability to see which way the wind blow, in public matters, and as he evidently anticipatet that all he had to bring be- fore the Board would not result in any action being taken at that meeting, he determined to say nothing. I underetand that another meeting is to be called to consider the same eubjec.t, and that it is likely the wcond dlscuesion will Mee be • lively one.

The members of the District Education Committee of the Widnes School Board have sent a communication to the Chairman of 1.1.`e Widnes Local Boani, orhiçtl wal read at the last meeting of that body, complaining of the had influence brought to bear upon the children of the district through the half-yearly pleasure fairs, the decrease in the average attendance at school during the fair week : and the immoral influence of the fairs upon the young. Tide letter has mi. dent!ar not received the sanction of the members of the Scheel Board, act body, and the question arises of whether it ought not to have done so before being forwarded by Mr. Denby the clerk, in his official capacity. The IGter rim to a warm discussion at the Local Board meeting, and Wesleyan vied with Congregationalist in condemning, in somes;hat unmeasured tGms, the influence of the fair, Mr. Brown's speech revealed the fact that about £29 was the amount realised from letting the and, but he stated that he felt quite sure that thus represented what was really a great toes to the neighbourhood, and that there wak not a shopkeeper in Anne-street, or Victoria-road, who would not be quite willing to subscribe to raise nacho sum if by doing an they could have the fair abolished. I cannot say that I feel quite as confident as Mr. Ilrown in the disinterested generosity of the shopkeepers of Anne-street and Waterloo- road, and their willingness to pay that • cermin SUPP..d , moral reault may be brought about. Perhaps Mr. Brown means that the shopkeepers imagine that they lose a goodly month, the Bedouin-like trader, who attend fairs, coming to the toyn, and that they would be willing to pay to keep them out. It wee a feeling a little akin to this which created touch a stir at Ephesus, when the makers of the silver Marines for Diana becatne convinced that their craft was in danger, and they raised 'a tumult, which lasted some hours, and during the whole of the time the shout went up te heaven—. Great is Diana of the Ephesians." Mr. Carey moved an amendment to the proposition'et Mr. Brown, that the prayer of the letter should be granted, and the sanction of the Board to mob half-yearly gatherings withdrawn. The! amendment was to the effect that the matter should he referred to the Markets' Committee for consideration. In the course of his speech on the subject he said that he had visited the fair and found very little drunkenness there. Ile also observed that the inspector of police had told him, in answer to an inquiry, that m far from there being an increase of drunkeonem by the holding of the fair. if anything, there were rather fewer cases at fair time than upon other °cm- 'ions. According to this remark:able statement the stall- holders, exhibjtors of human monstrositim, fat pigs, and other such like things ought to be awarded a medal of some sort by the temperance moiety for causing, if anything. a diminution of drunkenness. I am afraid the only medal such worthies would get if it were awarded on the ground of any such auppose,l merit, would bet lmther one. Where can the Inspector of Police have been on the nighte of a fair tone to arrive at such a remarkable conclusion Is Surely he cermet have had his eyes very wide open, or he must have been trusting to some subordinate's report. It is quite possible that there may not be a larger number of cases of drunkenness brought under the immediate reticent the Bench, as at a holiday time all police officers who are blessed with a little tact, permit of more freedom on the part of the disciples of John Barleycorn but I should most emphati- cally oppose any such ridiculous mere' naMment as that there is not mere drunkennessat a fair time than on ordinary days. Mr. Barrow supported the amendment, and took .a liberal view of the question, arguing that such amusements must be provided for the masses, and saying that it was far better to have the children upon the fair-ground than to have there "breaking windows in empty cottages, and in- dulging in games of that sort," M which pursuit, I have reason to believe, the sweet youth of Widnes show a remark- able pre-eminence. Mr. Barrow also very shrewdly said that all people were not lovers of tea meetings—a muffin_ fights," se some of the British workingmen hare the impu- dence to call rhem ImuststythisrenohforMr. Barrow, that I consider the workingman show, a wise discretion in avoiding some of the gatherings of this character, if he anews anything of the meet influences of a goal cop of too,

div.p: DESCRIPTION OF WIDNES SEWERAGE WORKS.

For eeveral years past the desirability of sewering the town of Widnes bee been under the consideratkn of the authorities, but the carrying out of miy plan has I,en front vear to rear adjourned. Probably the somewhat serious kttacks of zymotic disease from which certain tections el Widnes have suffered during the lad few years hare drawn the attention of those more immediately interested in the matter to the importance of carrying out a ...terse scheme fee the town, which is now gradually, but surely, extending on every side, and promises to be an extensive centre of population in years to come. Perhaps the rather exceptional difficulties which would besets be dealt with in semering a place the soil of which is so permeated with liquid from the great chemical works which rover such a vast portion of ire area, and the fear that those who faced the ratepayers with such a proposal would meet with anytlong but an encour- i aging reception have been GIUMS operating in favour of putting off any plan of the kind. We are, however. glad to eay that Mr. James Crow, who is the chairman of the Whine. Local Board—Lett, known as Major Cross—has taken the matter in hand, with the result that the scheme has already been subtnitted to the Local Government Board, and there is every prospect of its being approved. The proposal will deal with the whole of that part of Widnes which is west of the St. Helens railway, with the exception of West Bank. The sewer itself will extend from the Marsh brook to Sinn.. ('m, the nutlet being about three hundred yards were of I the Runcorn and Widnee viaduct. It will thee proceed ! front the Marsh brook outlet, under the viaduct of the !GA; e.„‘lo,oon N line onfrthZessatermue tnailny thoenthuenda.t.h.e. road J further to the Little Briton, at the eml of Sloordane thence *long Moor-lane to the police station thence to Anderson's corner, or what in better known as Kent's lamp, representing a distance of 1.000 yards. The sewer front the river to Kent's lamp will be egg-shaped, and aft. by 4ft. and from Kent's lainp to SIMITCP Crose aft. din. by 3fl (egg- shaped). The gradients are, by comparison with other large aewere, very good, and the lowest gradient will be self. eleansigg. The usual appliances for entering and clearraing the sewer will be provided. The ventilating arrangements will be superior to those generally met with in sewers, and will be specially adapted to the requirements of the district. The sewers will be fitted with ample flushing aptqratos, likewise specially adapted for the needs of the dietrict, the eon of which is composed to a large extent of chemical ttaate. The sewer will contain a Large quantity of chemical acids, and the sewers will. therefore, require special care in dmigning and constructing, as the materials generally used in the construction of such work will be out of the qoestion in this instance. The work will be carried out in detail by Mr. Wallace Copland, engineer of the sewerage works to the Board.

div.p: WHIT-MONDAY ..AT FROI,SHA.M.

Toe institution of Whit-Monday as a day for public demonstration of the friendly societies was again duly obo evened at Frosleham, and, as usual net such occasions, the main street was all alive with the accessories to the enjoy- ment of the fun of the fair. The clubs who walked in proces- sion to the church were the Forester, limits, and ()Mellows, ' each headed by • flag and a band of 111.1 e, the members wearing the ernhlents peculiar to the several societies to I o blob they belonged. On arriving at the sacred building the , eutvird each other in the rendering of the National Anthem. and not the least loyal were the church and chapel and fife bands, who looked eseceedingly well in their neat uniforms. The Rev. 11. R Blogg, vicar, conducted the • serv:ce, which consisted of the Commandments, and Epistle !and Gospel for the day. The hymns selected were Ancient : and Modern, 380, Bear ye one another's burden :" and 273, 1" Behold how wool and Joel ul a thing it is, brethren. to dwell , together in unity." The Vicar took for his tent the dth chapter of Epistle to Galatians. and 2ml verse, "Bear ye one !another's burdens, amt no fulfil the law of Christ :" and in , the course of his sermon the rev. gentleman remarked upon the appropriateness of the test, and dwelt upon the lemons to be drawn therefrom, vis., that we had all hardens to bear so that we should help each other to bear them, asd the motive which should guide us. They might all work out the law of Christ by sympathising 1 with those in distress, and so helping them to bear up under their particular burdens. The law of Christ was the law of love. All the towd done in the world, all noble deeds in a Dation's history, originated from the as of love, and he pointed out that their object in meeting there wrs• r•Ii0ou, one. the purpose of the societies being , n.-rt fur slice self-interests, but for the common benefit of the members. In conclusion he asked them to offer ups prayer that God woold blest their moieties and sow the wed of eternal life in the hearts of all who belonged to them, and to remember that as religious life n,r,essed. no they would prosper,and trusted that they n ;old bear in mind that religion was a bond which binds Cbristims more Mrether. The clubs visited the vicarage and the private residences of seyerel gentlemen who subscribe alavu.-div to the societies. The gardens at Castle Park--the seat nf E. A. Wright. Earl .2.P, —were kindly thrown opm to the public, and a largo nomber availed themselves of the opportunity of walking through this eylvan retreat, which is deserving of more notice than our space this week will allow.

WRIT-MONDAY AT PAILKOT. —The fine weather of Monday last attracted thousands of pleasure seekers by road and rail from Liverpool, St. Helena, and surrounding places, the greater part of whom betook themselves through the town of Preacot to well-wooded Knowsley and other adjacent rural retreats. The shops in Prescot were all closed and business wee entirely suspended. The streeta presented a very deeerted appearance during the day and the principal watchmakers shops being closed for the whole of The week afforded the chance of joining the numerous trips to various placee. div.head: MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY.
div.p: MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY.
SPEECI
LORD

A meeting of the more prominent members of the Con- ' eervative party, called by • circulor issued by Lord Beaconsfield, was held At Bridgewater House, C.eveland- square, St. James's, the town residence of the Earl of Elleemere, at three o'clock on Wedue.sday afternoon. The meeting was regarded as one of a strictly private character. The invitations sent out numbered about 550, and the affirmative responses case to within 100 of the number There were present the member. of the late Government, and a Loge eps inkling among Conservative 'ambers of ex- M.P.'s, who were defeated at the late election. The most rigid precantions were taken for the purpose of ensuring that the privacy should be absolute. The Earl of lI.CONSFIRLD, who was warmly received on tieing to addresa the meeting, expressed a hope that the proceedings would be regarded as of a strictly private and not of a public character. He referred to the sudden change which had taken place in the position of the party, which, although he admitted it was by no means expected, was not to be altogether regretted. He now no reasona to despair of the fortunes of the party, but, on the contrary, saw already eigns of hopefulness and encouragement. Although they were now on the Opposition side of the house, they possessed the power of a united party, which could not fail to exercise a considerable influence in the govern- ment of the country. If they were from to themselves and their principles he looked forward to their return to power at no distant period. He mferrel to the extraordinary opposition which their policy had encountered, and expremed surpri. Hat Mr. Gladstone, after the repeated expression of his desire to retire from the heat at political controversy, should have been prevailed upon to assurne the position of Prime Minister, and associate with it the arduous duties of the Chancellor of else Exchequer. (Cheers.) It would be unworthy of the Tory party to indulge in vain regrets because they had experienced:, viciesitude of fortune which, judged from the experience of the present, I the next election might probably convert into a signal I i triumph. (Cheers.) It had been rumoured that it wan hisi election to retire from the position with which he hod been so many years entreated bv the party, but Ise had never given the slightest ground for faith a supposition. (Cheers.) If those with whom it had kern alike his pleasure and honour to be so long associated considered that his reten- tion of the leaflet-o,lp would be of advantage to them, whatever ability be possessed would be devoted to their I service, in promotion of those grand constitutional princi- NIS to,nhict, thin country was indebted for continuity of its national history and the maintenance of its position to the s.le of nations. (Cheese.) He was satisfied that the Conservative party would profit by the experience of the ,late election in a more important, not to say essential, ! particular, and that wan the necessity for more perfect organimtion. The superiority of organization enjoyed be I the Liberal party was manifest in mat of the constituencies I during the recent contesta, but he hoped tlmt this weak ' point in the Conservative armour would Ise strengthened I before another appeal was made to the people. (Hear. hear.) I The late Government hail given up the seals of office to their successors wills the consciousness that they had done something to restore the prestige and in- fluence and maintain the honour of the country. They had able the satisfaction of knowing that they had done note little to promote the welfare of all claeses during a period of trade &premien without parallel in the 'mule of the nation. An enthusiastic Aslntirer of Cisnservative principles had prophesied that the present Liberal Govern- I meld woultl, notwithstandingits denunciation of their policy, 1 be inrealitv conservative, and he justified that expectation I on the attitude of wlmt had been designated 0 moderate I Liberalism." It must. however, be lorne in 'Med that this I view woe expressed before the formation of the present ad- minietration and the advent to exalted positions of gentle- , men who prid.el themselves upon what had recently been characterised as "destructive Radicalism." (Clieers.) The present Liberal Ministry was now, apparently. A happy end united family. Tile lion had lain 'lowa with the lamb ; per- versity had yielded, and acknowledged mildness. The past wash he forgotten. and the future made brilliant by a united display of Liberal and Radical fireworks. (Laughter) the difficulty WAS tut to know what the Liberals intended to to, but what they did not intend to do. Their programme I wee literally as wide as the poles. The aristocracy wae to be taken in had, the middle clams "vere to be looked to, and the remaining orders of society were to have boons and blessings showered upon them in an abundance only paral- leled in Eastern tales. Whether thisremarkableconsinnmation was ever to he obtained was the secret of the (snore, but he must confess ton tendency to scepticism, for he had passed the period of political childhood. With respect to the future of the Tory party, he strongly enforced upon all his adherents the need of unity. Although mince List he met a gathering of Conservatives the party was not numeri- cally ettong in Parliament, nevertheless, by united action they might do much towards the maintenance of principles which were dear to them, and which they believed to be the bent for the interests of the nation. lie recommended the party to maintain an attitude of dignified oppesition. To .s certain extent, Radicalism was for the present triumphant, but nothing would induce hint to believe that its success could be pertnanent. The entire history of the nation was opposed to such supposition. (Cheers.) He had with some amount of cit. endeavoured to trace the cause of the altered feelings which had come over the constituencies, and the conclusion at which he had arrived was that it was the result of I desire fern change of government, and not the coneequence of any dislike to Conserative principles, or any personal antipathy to the men wbo had been at the helm during the post six year.. He would not trouble them with process's of thought by which he had arra"d at this 0000I1Ini013, hut Ise could assure them that it I was a conclusion which had not been beefily ' adopted, and it was important that it should be tome in mittd for the future in dealing with the con- stitnencien. How the discordant elements brought together in the present Government were to retain their cohesion was a problem which he would not attempt to solve. Personally. he towsideverl it improwiLle for such a ministry to be of Meg duration, and he said this with due regard to the history of past administrations. He trusted that in 'speeches to their constituents Conservative members and those who had unfortunately lost their seats, ansoug whom he was pleased' to know a goodly number were present on that occasion, I would lose no opportunity of bringing before the electorsl Ilse fundamental principles of Conservatism. There wet on' that subject a great dell of miereprenentation, which it was the duty of every trod member of the party to strive to retnove. An boreal. appeared to prevail in many quarter. that Conserv:diens meant legislation for particular clam., and the making of law. in favour of those who were blessed with 'social advantages of no mean order whereas it was, in fact, a broad and compreheneive policy, which , aught to conserve all there was worth preserving in the institutions of the nation, and to introduce frosts time to time reforms having for their object the welfare and I happinas alike of all classes of the commuoity. (Cheers,) They were well aware of what the 'Conservative party hail accomplished in the interests of the nation, but those triumphs should Le steadily kept in the view of the people, aud their influence upon the position ad welfare of the nation brought prominently forward. The great marl characteristic' traits of Conservatiern should be continually demonetmted. He believed that the principles of Conservatism prevailed largely ainonget all clossea of Englishnsea. The Conservative workingman had been epoken of as a myth, and as being as extinct as the dodo. It had been said that Use Anserims caucus system had entirely obliterated the Conservative workingman, if he ever . hasl any existence. But lo did not believe coat Englishmen of any close would long allow their principles to Le dictated to them and their political action to Ise guided be anv rns- tern of machinery. He WWI convinced that 0 'strong leaven 1 pervaded the working classes and that the nebleet and best of thesn would be at all times found upholding the princi-1 ples of that which be had no hesitation in calling the eetional party. They might not alwase approve of every detail in the policy of the leaders of thAt party, but he wee satisfied that they would always be found stout defenders of its broad principle.. They had often given unmistakable evidence of their inherent attachtnent to Conservative I principles. Ile urges, all those who were listening to him tol owlet to the unnoet of Useir power in the orginination of the Conservative working classes. the was acquainted with several each organiamions, which had done much for else promotion of Conservative principles in different parts of the country, and he looked forward to them as one of the most certain means of securieg the (mere triumph of Conservatism. He woe pereuailed that many of the middle classes of the country had voted against the Coneervati, candidates through mis- conception MI to the causes of the depression of trade. No opportunity should be lost in removiug this misapprehension and in showing that the commercial 'Berens did not arise, as was alleged by their opponents, from any lack of pre- science or want of administrative uspacity on the part of the leaders of the Conservative party, but from uiumea beyond the control of any Government. lie expressed his satisfac- tion at seeing that the principles of the foreign policy of the Conservative Government, notwithstanding that it hail been so persistently misrepresented and so fiercely denounced, were likely to be carried out by their succasore, and he urged them, no longer the present Government in its foreign relations continued to maintain the interests and position of the country, to abstain from any factious opposition, butte give them a united and patriotic suprort. He vindicated the policy of the late Government as the ono hest adapted to the existing Mate of trade, and stated that the miscalcu- lation of the Indian accounte had taken them toy- surprise quite a emelt as any one else. He also expressed his pleasure at seeing present at the 'sleeting his noble friend the Earl of Carnarvon, who hail rendered signal service to the Conservative cause, and whose readiness to fight again in thee nks of the party with which he had been to long and no honourably connected was an additional assurance of its speedy return to power. Tlie noble earl, having spoken ePwardr of an hour, resumed his neat amidst prolonged cheering. The Duke of BUO'CLEI.IIII expresal his conviction that, although Mr. Gladstone hail Leen able to snatch a triumph in Midlothian, the victory was only traneitory. His son, Lon] Dalkeith, had been defeated, bet the Conservatives of Midlothian were wiser now than they were at the time of Ike election, and had already commeneed rectifying the weak points of their otganiation. It affonled him inexpressible pleasure to hear Lord Beaconsfield announce his willingness to continue the leadership of the party, and he had no doubt that under his skilful and prudent guidmee it wouLl hold its due position in the state. The Conservatives had been defeated owing to deficient party organisation end to whole- sale misrepresentation: and when the organisation had been correctod,and the mierepresentation bad been dispelled, they would be again victorious _

Si, R0131911T Poet. nbserv,sl that no one had been a greater victim to misrepresentation than he had—misrepresentation not only of the tongue. but of the pen. However, he was well accustomed to it, and instead of being disheartened, he found his spirits all the taller for it. It roused him to turn upon his assailants, and in eltposing their calumnies would be found the best means of outing the Conservative cause. He had lately crossed swonls with Sir William Harcourt, and he did not think that he got the worst of it, for he had the satisfaction of linos ing that he had done something to rescue Oxford from being any further misreprettented by that right honourable sad learned gentleman, who was now natal the House of Commons begging here awl begging there for a Seat. and 26 far with se little chance of finding' onee, the man lath, moon. (Laughter.) The honour of

Oxford had been redeemed, and no had that of Sandwich. I As the straw showed the direction of the wind, these elec- tions indicated that the electors found th.it they had already been "told" by the leader, of the Liberal party. Instead of men of mock-ate views, the Radical element predominated in the Ministry, and they were threatened with an avalanche of Lidice' crotchets of the moat advanced order. (Cheers.) The Duke of RICHMOND and Goan.rcc congratulated the meeting on the announcement of Lord Reec..nsfield's inten- tion to remain at the head of the piny. and he cordially agreed with what had fallen from the noble earl with refer- ence to its organition. DEATH OF MR. HINRY ASHWORTH.

The announcement of the death of Mr. Henry Ashworth will he received with widespread regret. For some time past Mr. Ashworth, who was in his Rath year, had been tra- velling on the Continent in the hope of restoring his health. Al Florence be was attacked, iii, said, by ROlll3ll f,ver, to which, according to a telegram received in Manchester on Tuesday morning, he succumbed on Monday night. Mr. Ashworth has cony and distinuguished claims to public remembrance. His aswciatlon with the Anti-corn- law I...ague and its leadtrs was not only intimate, hut in the highest degree influential ; and he gave the hest years of his life to promote measures of freedom, .• civil, religtems, and commercial." Along with his love of liberty he had an aversion to class privilege, which was very strongly ex- pressed, and which may perhaps be deemed especially sp. propri its to a man M whom :111CIFIll lineage was united with modern ideas of social justice. , , • , _ . . . .

His Quaker training did not preclude a touch of ancestral ! pride, a eirannistance that may be held to 'justify sumo brief particulars of Ili. family. The Aahwortlia con he traced back to the Conqueror'e time, and were certainly in pos- seasion, at a yery earls' period, of a grant of Ashworth town- ship, lying between R.lidale and Baty. They were " the Ashworths of Ashworth " for centuries, as they might have been to thia day bad their epirit of independence been less, and wealth tante valued by them than honorer. Some of Hem fought in the Parliamentary army against Charles 1., and at the time of the Cotiventicl, Act the Ashworth" be- came Dissenters. Their political and religion. opinions ex- posed them to frequent flues and punishment. Persecution made them comiewatively poor, and drove them from their old home. Thus it came about that to the reign of Charles 11, one portion nf the family settled in the Forest of Ros- amidst., while another migrated to Yorkshire; and it is from !these two sources tlmt the [waren of the name have spread and multiplied. One of the Hoesetal.le branch, to which Mr. Henry Ashworth belonged, went to London nn some busi- ness while the plague err raging, and he died there. His clothing and personal effects were sent home to Lancashire, and five of his relatives soon lay dead, baying been seised with the infection when the packages were opened. A for. thee family dispersion wae the c.sequence. One ,of the sons sold part of his Hossendale property, land settled at Turtoo, near Bolton, as a tenant farmer on the Oaks estate. Ilere the Ashworth', though they prospered both in agriculture and in trade, did not at heel increase in number, for the grandfather of Mr. Henry Ashworth was at one time the only cornicing member of that' branch of the family. Ile entered into business in Manche.- i ter, and an old Directory inentione him as the occupier of a warehouse in Doinsgate. Ile tend thre children his son follo hail eleven, and hie grandson Henry had eleven—six sons and live daughte's. Henry Asnworth, the immediate mbject of tide ,ernoir, was born September 4, 1794, and was the eldeat child of John and Isabel Ashworth. They were then residing on their own property at Bertenshaw, adjoining the estate of The Oaks above mentioned. The latter came into their posses. sion in 1820, when it was offered for ttale, and Mr. John Ashworth bought it. In course of time it deacended to his eldeat eon. Mr. Henry Ashworth inherited Rico, and extended, a cotton-spinning business in which Mr. John Ashworth bad latterly engaged, after having nrried on with success tlmt of fustian-cutting, which his father had nom- ' menced.

-.The—allied family of liMns claim also a passing note, as its genealogy discloses the Dm that the marriage of Mr. I Henry Ashworth nod M.. Letitia Mee, of Liverpool, which I took place in 1823, at Ilardshaw Meeting House, St. Helens —was that of two lineal dercendants of John and Abigail Hies, of Carlton Biggin. The history of this family, equally with that of the Ashwurths, record, the hereditary transmission of alerting qualities. It woe distinguished for devotion to religion and piety, if not for genius or wealth ; and ma of the family has therefore written of It that :•Tbe descendents of PO unpretending and devoted a lineof ancestry may adopt the language of the poet • My hyst to not that I detiwe my birth Fnuti lot ns enthroned, or rulers of the north: But higher far Inv proud pretentious The ten wn or parents past iitto the skies." Mr. Henry Anlrtrorth's comniercial training was received in great measure front hie father, in whose business he assisted from the age of If, after having attended several echools connected with the Society of Friends. He was for , a short time a school-fellow of kis lifedong friend Sir Thomas Bagley, Bart. After luring school, he engaged in hosMese, taking hie share with his brother Edmund in the mmagernent of their extensive mills at Turtnn. Here they maintained, at a great cost to the firm, excellent schools, with library and reading-room, in which many persons who sobselnently at- tained to wealth and position received their sole education, whilst others obtained remunerative engagements in private and public offices. Mr. Ashworth took a warm interest in politics from his earliest manhood. Nothing that affected the interests of "pence, retrenchment, and reform " could be to hints matter of indifference. The anti-slavery agitation, the extension of the franchise, the promotion of popular , education carninanded his keenest sympathies. Non-inter- vention in the internal affales of other countriee want cardinal point in his political creed, and the disestablish- mem of the English Church he advocated with untiring seal. lie at all times stubbornly refused to pay Church , rates. The monopoly in corn excited his SpeCIAI hostility, land in the establishment of the Anti-com-law League he , took :I prominent tort. It had no heartier supporter, either , by munificent pecuniary nil or indetatigxbie personal effort. He was a member of its Council through the whole of the I I iteration, and was actively concerned in all it, operations. I He was one of Mr. Cobden's most intimate friends, and largely assisted Mr. Braley. the late Mr. Stagg, and others in the several efforts that were made to recoup him for the pecuniary sacrifices imposed by his exclusive dermion to public affairs. The first or national subscription, which Irealised about £70,000, seems to have been absorbed be existing liabilities; the second effort, in 1860. amounted to 1.40.010 and a third waa made after Mr. Cohden's death Ifor the benefit of his family, which realised £24rtsi. The introduction of the great free-trade alvocate to his faithful friend took place at the Coion CIO, in the year 1837. old: ono of the first of their joint enterprises was the holding of a great meeting in favour of a national system of education. I Early in 1810 it sae arlanged that deputations front various . Intone should uesenthic in London M procure interview, on the subject of Corn Law repeal with the Pretnier, Lord Ilethourne, and certain members • of hi. Cibinet. The Premier's curt remark woo that 4 repeal was impossible,' and Sir Robert Peel and Sir James Graham gave no encouragement loth, deputies. In his interenting and vale. able " History of Cobden and the League," Mr. Ashworth thus relates Sir balle/I'll frigid reception of himself and his collerigues."Thedvputation seemed to heir no way acceptable ' to Sir James Graham. Ile was perverse and captious noon extent which we could only account for as the consequence of some severe commentaries which had appeared from one ' t of our lecturers who had been in the neighbourhood of his I estates. • • When Mr. John Brooks descritul the dis- tress in the cotton trade, Sir James retorted that the con- sumption of cotton was greater than at any previous period, , and Mr. Thomas Ashton replied that the dependants were I more numerous tlt.a at my previous perial, and that csarser I yarns were being spun. • • My turn .me next, and I . exclaimed against the injustice of restricting the import of food in onler to uphold rents, showing that the inevitable . effect would be to increase the non,. of unfair treatment' which was now felt by the people, and which it behoved every sten-wisher of his country not to disregard. At this point Sir James called out-- Why. yeti are a leveller,' and I in an insolent tone inquired 'whether Ite was to jure that I the labouring classes had some claim to the landlords' estates a' Being somewhat startled. I appealed to my col- leagues as to whether anything I hal said supported such an idea, when Mr. Thomas Ashton called out, `Go on, Mr Anhworth, and never mind what he has said: Sir James, in reply to the denotation, gait' that if the Corn Laws were re- mated great trusters would fall upon the country, that thy land would go out of cultivation, that Church and State could not be upheld, that all our inatitutions would he re- duced to their primitive elements, and that the people we were exciting would pull down oar houses about our ears. We responded lath. effect that to uphold nor institutions we must remove injustice, that we had no fear for our own houses, and that, whatever might become of the Established Church, we had no fear for religion." With various friends Mr. Ashworth subeequently waited on Earl Fitswilliam. Lenin Radnor, Clarendon, and Lanedowne, and explained the principle, and objects of the League. He cans assed for subscriptions towards its funds among the merchant class mn London, till, as he said, there woe hardly Intone in , Wood-strut on whicb he had not trodden in pursuit of our , object." In company with Messrs. Cobden and Bright, he visited in 1543 some of the most highly cultivated parts of Durham, Northumberland, Camberland.and Gat Lothian to obtain sound information on the position of agriculture and the views of the fanner.. During their absence or I this tour they vrere often humorously referred to rto reference to the initial lettere of their names) no "the A B C of the Lea,ue gone to study farming." In 1845 a Committee of the House of Lords met to inouire into the pressure of local taxation on landed property, before which Mr. A,..n .4th gave evidence to prove the ententeo of an inequality of local rating in Lancashire which wan unfair to owners of factories and other commer- cial property and unduly favourable to the owners of land.' On the 211 rd December, 1845, at a great meeting held in the I

Manchester Town HAIL Mr. Ashworth moved a revolution to the effect that eto promote the a.,it ttion for corn law rep.l a sum of £.250,00 should so raieed." His epeech was : animated and succeesful. and this bold challenge won onani- j mond,' accepted. Exertione like these we, continued with ! unflagging zeal till rewarded by the abolition of the corn ! laws, and the final meeting of the League wari held 00th, Sod of July,lB4B. in the Manchester Town Hall. One of the moat , valuable portions of his book is his account of the negotia. tion of this Treaty. He points out that -*bile the Emperor • Napoleon paid Cobden every attention, appointing him a commissioner, with French expert. to assist him, Cobden IFIS hampered by the English tiovernment that had sent hint as its representative. " Certain it is," he remarks, o that Mr. Cobden, whilst very earnestly engaged on the affsirs of Lis iniesion, began to receive front certain members ! of the Cabinet marks of obstructive treatment, and letters t which indicated an impression. not to say no expecMtion, that hemight tn well resian his position and abandon Lis pnrpose. div.head: '1 TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT AN IRON WORKS. PEILSONB KILLED.
div.p: '1 TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT AN IRON WORKS. PEILSONB KILLED.

A frightful accident, by which 23 men net their occurred at the work. of the Birchill Hall Iron Company, Wale&II, on Saturday. lheae works contain a numlwr of pudding furnaces, connecter with three "egg-ended vertical boilers," EAcI. weighing about 30 tone. Between ten and eleven o'clock, while *lout 50 men were busily working around it, the middle boiler soddenly shot up from its bed ton height of about 21%) feet. thi its way it parted into two pieces, one-half being driven forwards for 00 yards, and the other backwards for a distance of 150 yards through the chintney-stack and over the canal which runs at the back of the works. lnaide the shed, the escaping etearn and water, coming in contact with the molten metal, caused it to explode and scatter all over the place, bringing with it the brick and iron work of the surrounding furnaces. The chimney-stack also fell upro the shod. the deatruction of which it completed, and upon the mat, where it sank aeveral boats. Instant parts of tile works were also damaged by the flying debris. When assistance was obtained and an entnmce effected into the ruin, it was found tl.t 12 men had been killed outright. Their bodies were so frightfully mangled that they appeared as though they hod been blown from a canoon's mouth. Every roan near the boiler at the time of the explosion was injured, and the position of those not killed was horrible in the extreme. Ihe rubbish which cot cred the sufferers was or intensely hot that it could not be immediately removed, and thus, although or,asionally a man could be seen and spoken to, there was no possibility of his immediate rescue. One wretched fellow was lying for some time beneath a mass of wrecka.ge sith stream of scalding water pouring upon him. Ire noise of the explo- sion alarmed the neighbour hood, and th.. place was non surrounded by • crowd of excited women, whose agony of apprehension added greatly to the painfulness of the
Two more of the perm. injured by the boiler explosion at Walsall dicxl on l'uend,, making 25 deaths in all. It is estimated that £12,000 will be required for the relief of the survivors.

Of the 15 survivors of the boiler explosion at Walsall 14 were better on 'Tuesday, though throe of the number were deemed in a critical condition on Sunday. The fifteenth Aurviver is not expected to recover. The father of one of the deceased failed to identify bin, until after examining the body aeveral times. Nothing so far lias tranapired account. ins for the explosion. The inquest on the persons killed wan opened on Tuesday afternoon. The coroner and jury visited thcl worka, and made a minute inspection of the fraginents of the boiler, which were found to be corroded and thin in parts. The inquiry woe adjourned till Friday, when the evidence of Mr. Marten, of Stoutbridge, will be taken at the instabce of the coroner, and the evidence of one or more expel ts at the instance of the town autborittes. The deceased were buried on Wednesday. The proprietors of the works defray all expenses.
