div.head: WHITSUNTIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE AT WIDNES.

There are very few towns M tie rowdy Palatine where] there ere et, few demonstrations of Clubs and Sunday-schoole at the season of Whitsuntide ..at Widnee. Owing to the place being within a shilling ride of the gleatest seaport in I th wrrld, with its miles of docks and its attractions at New Brighton, Birkenhead, Emitham, and other resorts of pleasure urhe,, and the comparative nearness of Southport, with its Whlter Gardens, and Manchester with its wondrous pro- of Sunday-schools and its never failing Belle V. and Po ens, the aim of the greet majority of Widnes's°, at Whitsuntide appears to be to get as far. they possibly can from the marvellous smells which permeate the air of the mon and neighbourhood. They leave the railway stations by , hundreds and thousands, and may be met with in all sorts, al queer, farmway nooks, trying fore few hours La inhale I the sweet country breezes and to peep once more at the violets and the prirnrosea. There is one advantage, if one it can be called, to those who have to reach Witham by a late night train for if the weary traveller or excursionist has dropped nearly off to ffeep, his olfactory organs will tell hire in an instant that he is within the reach of salt-cake

...,.,. ...- once more.. About 5,000 people passed over Runcorn railway footbridge on Whit. Monday, being nearly 1,500 more than last year. The weather TIM IA a transcend. ently beautiful character, there being scArcely a cloud in the sky, and the air being tempered hy a gentle breeze. The views from the bridge were lovely in the extreme, owing to the great clarity of the atmosphere. From one side might be seen the beautiful outlines of the Welsh mountains, whilst from the other could be discerned Halton Castle and tb, estate of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart. The river was alive with small craft filled with happy looking excursionists eager to get a glymps ol the various ship-building yards, and c..my of them appeared to be busy telling ••the old old tale" of love to the suggestive sound of the bells of the Parish church, which Mao beautiful for situation. In the distance streets tithe gaunt looking town might be heard the strains of various heeds; liege fluttered gaily in the breeze from most of the public buildings, and the bannera carried by the Sur,day school children gave Runcern a very interesting appearance. Harking back once more to the Lancashire side of the water, we may say that an excursion train was run Boni the Central atation to Belle hoe, and there were about 500 passengers. The London and North-Western alss ran a trip to the same place, and their station was filled with passengers all the I livelong day. Early in the afternoon the members of the . Zion Band of Hope met at their schoolroom, Oohed-street, and, heeded by the Warrington trotted Brass Band, paraded Oho principal streets, carrying numerous flags and bannerets., 00 their return to the schoolroom a tea meeting wss held,' alter which songs and recitations were given by the children, under the presidency of Mr. T. Burrows.

div.head: WIIITUNTIDE IN RUNCORN.
div.p: WIIITUNTIDE IN RUNCORN.

This year the lovers of Whitsuntide in Runcorn, were Immured with niost lovely weather, on Sunday and Monday. Scarcely a cloud was to be seen in the azure vault overhead, and • pleasant breeze made walkirg a pleasure. On Mon- day the various places of business in the town were closed, and Irons an early hour until far into the afternoon there woo nothing to be heard but the sea eral bands of music and the belle of the parish church. Ihnusands of visitors found their way into the town by rail and on foot. Indeed, it is many years since the streets were so crowded with pleasure seeker; who seemed to be everywhere, and to be revelling in the glorious sunshine and completely given up to the Boise of enjoyment. Upwards of 5,000 people crossed Ituncurn railway footbridge during the day, being about 1,500 more then last year. The usual precemions at this season were fully as well patronised as in previous years, if, indeed, they were not more popular, and we give details of them below. On Sunday there was theusual gathering of the Primitive Methodist, in the form of a camp meeting on Runcorn Hill. A great number of people were present, the weather beingof a most propitious description and two highly succesaful meetings took place. In the evening the members of the mine body held a lovelmst in their tine chapel in Cireenway- road, when there was a good attendance. On Monday morning the oiennial gathering of the Inern- bere of the secret orders of the tu,irn took place in Devon- shire square, and excited great pt blic interest. The Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds (No. 777,) mustered to the num- ber of about 130, and proved the special feature of the pen. cordon, as they generally do upon this occasion. They were headed by the banner of the lodge and the Northwich Volunteer Maas band, in uniform The officers and mem- bers wore beautiful !bashes, and carried the custoinary in- signia ; but the principel interest of the great body of spectators was centered in a luny, drawn by two horses, and decorated almost attractive manner. In the middle of the conveyance were persons representing a shepherd and shepherdess, and at the four corners were placed four children carrying bannereta, on which were the words "Faith," "Hope," "Charity," and "Unity." In the bind part of the wagon was nian wearing a bear skin aod lmding a dog tn a leash. f lie Grand United Order of Oddfellows were, as usual, strongly represented. " The Pride of Runcorn Lodge " (No. 39) was headed by the banner of the lodge and the Ditton brass bant, and the mem- ber, numbered about no, wore the sashes of the order and carried insignia. The Itteinbers of "The Lily of the Volley' Lodge (No. 515) numbered about 60, and were pre- ceded by the mpital band of the Runcorn Volunteers in uniform. The members wore the cust.mary sashes and carried ineignia. The" Duke of Edinburgh.' Lodge of the same ord. No. 027) were piment, to the number of about 90, and were headed by the Present Volunteer brass band in uniform, and the lodge banner. The processioa moved in the above order, down High sired and up R idge-street to Halton, where refreshments were provided, and various amusements were indulged in on the green of the Halton Castle Hotel. Early in the afternnon the members re-formed in procension, and they returned to Runcorn. THR DUKE'S CLUB AT TOR PARISH CHURCH. The members of the Duke's Club assembled to the number of 00000 250, at the Big House, Bottom Locke, and a proces- sion of goodly proportions was formed, which, headed by the nand belonging to the lodge, and the Widnes Good Templar brass band, walked to the Vicarage. They then proceeded to the Parish Church, where the Rev. Canon B Imlay, WA.. preached from Genesis axis chap. 20 verse," And Jamb aerved seven years Inc Rachel; and they seemed unto him bole few days, for the love lie had to her.' The reverend gentleman remarked that the last tiine Ice addressed them was from the 15th verse of the same chapter, when lie attempted to show them how Loom. the commodity of which the working had to dispose, was subject to the ordinary laws of aupply and demand, wages rising when the labour- market was undermanned, a rid fal ling when it was overstocked. He contrasted the patience with which Jacob served seven years for Rachel with the impatience which often characterised young couple, when they desired to enter on the marriage state. He argued in favour of marriage in the case of young people being postponed for a few years, in order that the interval might be employed in saving. The Canon con- cluded his retnarks by an earnest appeal to his hearers to mka as touch pains in providing against their spiritual wants as they did in making provision against sickness, old age, anil death. The prayers were read by the Rev. G. S. Simp- son, and the special lesson by Mr.Oldfiald, one of the officials of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. THE SCHOOLE—METHODIST, PRRERETENIAR AND CON- DEROATIONALIST.—EarIy on Monday afternoon the children attending the Method ist,St. John 's Presbyterian, a nd Bethesda Congregational schools assembled at their various buildings, in order to march through the town. They were preceded ny their respective ministers and superintendents, and walked in the following nrderi--Brunswick 'Wesleyan Sunday school (established 18001, numbering, with scholars, teachers, and friends, about 600; St. John's Presbyterian (established 1818), about 195; Bethesda and Sr. Luke's Congregational schools (established 1835), about 180; Primitive Methodist (established 1839), about 220; Ellesmere-Oreet United Methodist Free Church school, numbering 230 ; Mill-brow (Hallon-road) Wesleyans (established 1845), numbering 380; Camden school (established 1982), numbering nbout 1130; and Nelson-street (a branch of Camden Wesleyan estaolishrd 1878), about 130. The schnlars and friends, in no spirit of Christian union very pleasant to witness, all went into a field near the cenntery, where they tad VADOUR games, and were provided with tea. Sr. Enwartn's ROMAN CATROLIC Dee SCROOGE—The childien of these ',amnia assembled at Mill-brow at about nalf-past one o'clock, and, after forming in procession, walked to Halton, where they enjoyed themselves in various games, after which they returned to the schoolroom at Runcorn, where they gave recitations and reading, during •the evening. Pentair Cnrucx SCHOOLE—The scholars and friends .net about one o'clock, and were joinel by those-belonging to Newtown Mission School. They formed in procession, and, headed by their beautiful banner and the Widnes Hood Templar brass band, marched to the Vicarage, and from there to Runcorn Hill, where the afternoon was spent in • very enjoyable manner. On returning to the Vicarage the oroceaston was re-formed and returned to the National .4chools, in Church-street, where tea wan provided. After tea the teachem, elder scholars, and friends engaged in dancing, and overy pleasant evening was spent. Tawny Cnceen Scooora.—The scholars and friends connected with this school met at the room in Poole-lane about one o'clock, and headed by the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., Ind the mnior warden, marched to Duke's-field, ivhere they engaged in games, and afterwards retnmed to the achool- -nom, where tea woe provided.

Wesleyan Methodist (Waterloo-street) Branch To stand in Hardehaw-street, following &MOIL The procession was nether late at starting, it being nearly two o'clock before the walk commenced, although one o'clock was the time fixed. The procession went by Shaw- greet, Raven-street, Church-street, Bridge-street, Liver pool- road, Cropper's Hill, to the Queen's Park, again (kindly lent for the occasion by Conncillor W. H. Foster.) 'nail cases the girls walked first, the little ones leading. Amongst the processionists were the Rees. W. C. Taylor (Bantis:), i T. Virilshaw (Primitive), and H. J. Weatherhead (United Methodist.) Immediately before the procession started prizes were awarded for the three neatest, cleanest, and best temente, in the horses and carts, the judges being Messrs. J. B. Leach and J. Hamilton. After the inspection the following awards were made,—lst prise, a copper kettle, Union Plate Glass Company 20d, a copper kettle, Messrs. Doulton Brothers, 3rd, London and North-Western Railway Com- pany. An extra prize was given for a cart belonging to Messrs. Pilkington Brothers. the miter being Mr. James Glover. A special prize was alev given to Mr. T. Birchall, farmer, Huyton. The horses and carts hnd the duty of conveying the very young children to the field along with provision', &c. Arrived at the park games were at once , indulged in, the popular ones ..twat budding manhood and womanhood being the kissing ring, jolly miller, and French tig, or two's and three'a. as it is sometimes These games were kept up with great spirit throughont tbe day, and evidently gave great adisfaction to all participants, and indeed to lookers on. An exciting "game,' if eo it may be called, was one which 1739 monopolised by the I sterner sex. This was played IT tire or six young men, who were placed behind each other, the first ono receiving the " taps" (or blows perhaps is the more appropriate term) from those immediately behind him. The recipient of the blow has then to pck out the man who hit him, and it he succesaful the giver of the knock has to submit to the I indi:nity of being led round to the front by the ears: if he I is not successful, but picks out the wrong one, he has to be 'taken round in the same way and pay the penalty for the lack of his intuition. The natural consequence was that there were many unnaturally red ears. Swings were erected for the youngsters, and these were well patronised. The children were supplied with refreshments. During the afternoon balloons, representing various animals, were sent up, to the evident delight of the youngsters, who watched them soar away until they became invisible. There was the usual brass band and fife and drum band contests. The Pemberton band, having won the prize at previous contesta, was not allowea to compete, but was pre- genteel with a certificate stating the victories won on former: occasions. The Ravenhead band was the only one who put au appearance in the brass hand contest, and the prize—a ' side drum or kettle driim—was awardea to it. Two fife bands—Christ Church, Eccleaton. and the Presbyter'. band —competed for the prise to be given to the band which ' manipulated the fife moat akilfully. and the victory was won by the band in connection with Chriet Church, Ercleston. Mr. John Makin acted as judge of the fife bands, and Mr. Slobs, of Huyton, decided Iwtween the brass bands. The speaking cosiest formed a very interesting feature in the efternoon's proceedings. A long time elapsed before candi- dates were forthcoming, but as Mr. Leach said, the difficulty was in getting the first 0100 00 the platform, for on the first speaker having entered there was not much difficulty in getting others to follow. James BrOWII, of 1133-dock. the first to speak; Richard Wareing. of Parr, the aecend; John Turner, of Pemberton, the neat and Thorns, Anderton, of Pemberton, the last. The third mentioned received the I prise, there being not much difficulty in deciding. Mr. Lindon acted as chairman of this contest, and we understand that Mr. Weatherhead was the judge. The prize was recopy of "The Devil's Chain," by 51r. Jenkins. The refreshment stalls were under the management of Mr. NorYmgeour, who gave the greatest satisfaction. It RA9 computed that about 4,000 Rind of Hope children were present, but the number on the field was greatly above that.

THE CATHOLIC SCHOOLS. Whit-Monday, as aerial, was fully observed by the Catholic denomination in St. Helens. The education question is ever stimulating the leaders to renewed action and with the face of a School Board this is not to he wondered at. The resi.,cted rector of the district. Father I'llathorne, is con- tinually moving in the direcHen of advancement ainong the young branches of bin flock, and hi 3 energies have been tried to the utmost during the last few years. Schools have been required and been provided for in almost every quarter of the borough through his instrumentality, and yet he is called upon to provide further accommodation. The numerous buildings for scholastic purposes now erected in various parts of the town stand as monuments to his untiring industry. Lowe House, Gerard's Bridge, Holy Cross, and Parr are indebted to his indefatigable labonrs to provide Ins the increasing want. of the rapidly-growing
